title: Week 14 — Pitch & Review
text:
Format: 10-minute pitch to panel + 5-minute Q&A
Panel composition: course instructor + one external guest (industry practitioner where possible).

title: Week 14 — Pitch & Review
text:
Pitch requirements
Your pitch must cover:
1. The business problem and why it matters (quantified where possible)
2. The solution and how it works (non-technical explanation required alongside technical)
3. ROI estimate with stated assumptions
4. Risks: what could go wrong, what the model cannot do
5. What happens next — what would a real deployment look like?

title: Week 14 — Pitch & Review
text:
Q&A handling
The Q&A challenges business assumptions, not just technical choices. Students must defend why they made the decisions they did.

title: Week 14 — Pitch & Review
text:
Peer review
Each team evaluates one other team’s pitch using a structured rubric. Graded for quality of feedback.

title: Week 14 — Pitch & Review
text:
Deliverables

Pitch deck
Peer review feedback

title: Week 12 — Scoping & Business Case
text: The business case must be approved by the instructor before week 13 begins. This gate prevents over-engineering and forces students to think before they build.

title: Week 12 — Scoping & Business Case
text:
Business case requirements
Your document must include:
- Problem statement (precise, not vague)
- Target user and how they will interact with the output
- Success metric (one primary KPI)
- ROI estimate — even a rough one requires assumptions to be stated
- Data source and known limitations
- Risks and ethical considerations

title: Week 12 — Scoping & Business Case
text:
Deliverable

Signed-off business case document

title: Week 10 — Demand Forecasting & Supply Chain
text: Format: Lecture + project

title: Week 10 — Demand Forecasting & Supply Chain
text:
Topics covered

Time series decomposition: trend, seasonality, noise — reading each component
Moving average and exponential smoothing — intuitive explanation before any formula
Facebook Prophet for business forecasting: appropriate use cases and known limits
Forecast error metrics reframed as business costs: MAE and MAPE expressed in euros, not percentages
Inventory optimisation: Economic Order Quantity, safety stock, service level targets
The asymmetric cost curve: why being out of stock is typically more expensive than overstock

title: Week 10 — Demand Forecasting & Supply Chain
text:
Project
A retail chain needs to plan orders for next month across 3 product lines (stable, seasonal, volatile). Students:
1. Build a forecast for each product line
2. Recommend order quantities with a safety stock rationale
3. Quantify the cost of over- vs under-ordering using provided cost data
4. Write a one-page supply recommendation addressed to the operations manager

title: Week 10 — Demand Forecasting & Supply Chain
text:
Tools
Prophet, statsmodels, pandas — focus on reading and interpreting output correctly

title: Week 10 — Demand Forecasting & Supply Chain
text:

Forecast notebook with commentary
Order quantity recommendations per product line
Supply memo to operations manager (1 page)

title: Week 8 — Pricing & Revenue Optimisation
text: Format: Lecture + simulation exercise

title: Week 8 — Pricing & Revenue Optimisation
text:
Topics covered

Price elasticity of demand — intuition, how to measure it, and where it breaks down
Dynamic pricing: how Uber, airlines, and hotels do it, and why
Discount strategy analysis: short-term revenue gains vs long-term customer behaviour change
Segmented pricing: willingness-to-pay differences and ethical price discrimination
Revenue management: yield optimisation basics for capacity-constrained businesses
The promotional trap: when frequent discounting destroys margin permanently

title: Week 8 — Pricing & Revenue Optimisation
text:
Simulation exercise
Scenario: an e-commerce brand is considering a 10% price cut across its main product line. Students:
1. Use provided elasticity data to estimate demand change
2. Model revenue impact across 3 customer segments (price-sensitive, loyal, occasional)
3. Account for margin impact, not just topline revenue
4. Deliver a go / no-go memo with a quantified recommendation

title: Week 8 — Pricing & Revenue Optimisation
text:
Tools
pandas or Excel for scenario modelling — emphasis on interpreting the numbers, not the tooling

title: Week 8 — Pricing & Revenue Optimisation
text:

title: Week 6 — Product Analytics & Funnel Diagnosis
text:

Funnel analysis: signup → activation → purchase → retention — reading the drop-offs
Cohort analysis: how to read retention curves and what they tell you about product health
Session analysis: time-on-task, rage clicks, and behavioural drop-off signals
Feature impact analysis: did this release actually change user behaviour?
North Star Metric — choosing the one number that best captures product health
Communicating product findings differently to engineering vs marketing stakeholders

title: Week 6 — Product Analytics & Funnel Diagnosis
text:

A SaaS onboarding funnel: 60% of users drop off at the email verification step. Students receive an event log dataset and must:
1. Run funnel analysis and build the conversion chart
2. Generate ranked root-cause hypotheses, backed by evidence from the data
3. Write a product change recommendation with an estimated lift in conversion

pandas, plotly (event-log manipulation, funnel chart)

title: Week 4 — Data Visualization & Executive Storytelling
text:
Topics covered

Choosing chart type from the business question, not the data shape
The SCR structure for data narratives: Situation → Complication → Resolution
Dashboard design for decision-makers, not analysts
Common chart crimes: dual axes, 3D pie charts, truncated y-axes, and why they mislead
Annotation and narrative — making charts argue a point, not just display one
When to use a table instead of a chart

title: Week 4 — Data Visualization & Executive Storytelling
text:
Case study
“Sales dropped 15% last quarter — explain why and propose actions.”
Students receive raw data (not pre-built charts) and must:
1. Explore and diagnose the drop
2. Build a 5-slide executive deck for a fictional CEO briefing
3. Deliver a 5-minute live presentation — timed, with interruptions and questions
The interruptions are intentional: students must defend a recommendation, not just present slides.

5-slide executive deck
5-minute live presentation
Graded on: clarity of recommendation, visual choices, ability to handle Q&A

title: Week 2 — Problem Framing & Data Quality
text:

Problem decomposition: from vague business goal to a precise, answerable question

Selection bias and survivorship bias, with concrete industry examples
When “we don’t have the data” is itself a meaningful insight
Data dictionary creation — building shared vocabulary between analysts and stakeholders

Students receive a deliberately dirty e-commerce dataset. Tasks:

3. Write a one-paragraph data readiness memo addressed to a fictional manager

pandas, missingno

text:
📅 Curriculum

⊞ Grid View
☰ List View












Week 1 — ML Foundations & Workflow


What is ML? Supervised vs Unsupervised vs Reinforcement Learning












Week 2 — Data Preprocessing & Pipelines


Handling missing data, detecting outliers












Week 3 — Math & Information Theory


Linear algebra review: vectors, dot products, matrix multiplication












Week 4 — Linear Models for Regression


Linear Regression: formula, interpretation, closed-form solution












Week 5 — Logistic Regression & Classification


Logistic function, decision boundaries, sigmoid












Week 6 — Model Evaluation


Regression metrics: MAE, MSE, RMSE, R²












Week 7 — Bias–Variance Tradeoff


Underfitting vs overfitting; bias-variance decomposition












Week 8 — Data Sampling & Validation Techniques


Hold-out split, stratified sampling












Week 9 — k-Nearest Neighbors


KNN for regression and classification












Week 10 — Decision Trees


Splitting criteria: Gini, Entropy












Week 11 — Random Forests & Bagging


Bagging: theory and bias reduction












Week 12 — Boosting Algorithms


Boosting concepts: ensemble of weak learners












Week 13 — Modern Boosting Libraries


XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost












Week 14 — Feature Engineering & Feature Selection


Custom transformers, interaction features












Week 15 — Imbalanced & Noisy Data


Resampling: SMOTE, undersampling












Week 16 — Clustering & Dimensionality Reduction


Clustering: K-Means, DBSCAN, Hierarchical












Week 17 — Neural Networks & MLPs

title: Week 11 — Data Ethics, GDPR & the EU AI Act
section: Why this deserves a full week
text:
Why this deserves a full week
Every French and EU employer expects data scientists to know this material from day one. The EU AI Act is now in force. GDPR has been enforceable since 2018. Algorithmic bias is not just an ethical concern — it is an employment law and liability issue. Students who cannot speak to these topics will struggle in French job interviews.
crumbs: Week 11 — Data Ethics, GDPR & the EU AI Act

title: Week 11 — Data Ethics, GDPR & the EU AI Act
text:
Topics covered

GDPR article-by-article: what it concretely bans for a practising data scientist
EU AI Act: high-risk AI system classification and what compliance looks like in practice
Algorithmic bias as legal liability — the basics of EU discrimination law
Data monetisation: what a company can and cannot sell or share without consent
Privacy-preserving techniques: anonymisation, pseudonymisation, and a conceptual intro to differential privacy
The right to explanation under GDPR Article 22 — and what it demands of model design
crumbs: Week 11 — Data Ethics, GDPR & the EU AI Act

title: Week 11 — Data Ethics, GDPR & the EU AI Act
text:
Debate format
Case: a French company has built an automated CV-screening tool. Evidence emerges that it systematically ranks women lower in technical roles.
Teams of students argue one of three positions:
- Deploy with guardrails — propose specific technical and process mitigations
- Do not deploy — argue on legal and ethical grounds with specific article citations
- Redesign from scratch — propose an alternative system that would be compliant
All positions must cite specific GDPR articles or EU AI Act provisions. Vague ethical arguments are not accepted.
